steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing REFT, a resource-efficient federated training framework for heterogeneous, resource-constrained IoT and edge devices. Motivate federated learning and its communication and resource problems, then introduce our approach and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Deep learning needs lots of data; data is decentralized; Federated Learning
- How FL communicates and why it is costly; protocol-level work
- Open questions: communication rounds, bandwidth, privacy, constrained clients
- REFT: variable pruning + knowledge distillation
- Contributions
- Overall summary

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - deep learning progress: image classification, natural language processing
  - complex DNN models need massive data; works in centralized setting with access to all data
  - distributed systems with IoT and edge devices: data inherently decentralized
  - collaborative training hard: technical intricacies, privacy, data ownership
  - FL: distributed training on decentralized data, preserves privacy
- FL communication
  - iterative sharing of model parameters or gradients between Internet-connected clients (IoT, edge) and remote central server in cloud
  - protocols: TCP or UDP (cite), or other application layer protocols (cite)
  - each round: client trains locally, sends parameters; server aggregates with traditional aggregation methods
  - many client-server round trips -> more bandwidth, lower communication efficiency
  - hard in resource-constrained environments, e.g. smart home with IoT/edge devices, limited hardware, simplified web infrastructure; privacy equally important
  - research (cite) optimizing application layer protocols: less communication time, less packet loss; MQTT, AMQP, ZMTP
- Open questions
  - still: many bidirectional rounds, size of each update, privacy
  - Q1: FL with fewest rounds, minimal bandwidth per exchange, optimized network traffic, while preserving privacy?
  - clients far more constrained than data center servers: processing power, memory, storage
  - Q2: efficient FL as IoT/edge devices spread, optimize per-client resources, diverse devices, complex DNNs?
- REFT
  - Resource-Efficient Federated Training: variable pruning + knowledge distillation
  - pruning by client computational capacity; distillation for communication efficiency and privacy
  - inspired by FedKD (cite), which uses public dataset for privacy
  - asynchronous updates + public data -> less communication and privacy risk
  - experiments: big reductions in parameters, FLOPs, bandwidth; accuracy comparable to existing FL
- Contributions
  - variable pruning: pruning level per client by available resources; one-shot structured pruning of initial weights at server; less compute/communication overhead (or acceptable level); suits constrained devices
  - one-way, one-shot client-to-server knowledge distillation with unlabeled, non-sensitive public data; better communication efficiency; heterogeneous architectures after structured pruning can participate
- Summary: variable pruning + one-shot distillation -> efficient, effective FL for constrained devices, better client resource use, diverse architectures

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has made a lot of progress recently in many domains, including image classification and natural language processing, among others. But training complex Deep Neural Network (DNN) models needs massive amounts of data. Training with large data volumes works well in centralized scenarios, where the model can access all of the data. However in most cases, especially in distributed systems with Internet-of-Things (IoT) and edge devices, the data resources are decentralized by nature. This decentralized distribution of data makes collaborative training difficult, mainly because of technical intricacies, privacy concerns, and the intricacies of data ownership. Federated Learning (FL) has come up as a promising solution to these problems, because it allows distributed model training on decentralized data while keeping the data private.

FL techniques allow collaborative training by sharing model parameters, or gradients, again and again during training. The communication is between client devices connected to the Internet, which include IoT and edge devices, and a central server that is remote in the cloud, and together these form an FL-based system. Usually this exchange is done over common protocols like TCP or UDP, or other application layer protocols. After every round of training on its local data, a client sends its model parameters to the central server, and the server aggregates the parameters from all the clients using traditional data aggregation methods. But this iterative process needs a lot of back-and-forth communication between client and server, so bandwidth consumption goes up and communication efficiency goes down. This is a big hurdle for building efficient FL-based systems, especially in resource-constrained environments like smart home setups with IoT and edge devices that have limited hardware resources and simplified web infrastructure. It is challenging to use FL effectively in these applications while also treating data privacy as equally important. To reduce communication bottlenecks in these FL scenarios, some research has worked on reducing communication time and packet loss by optimizing application layer protocols. They look at Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), and ZeroMQ Message Transport Protocol (ZMTP) to make data exchange more efficient.

- Remaining challenges: many bidirectional rounds, update size, privacy
  - Q1: fewest rounds, minimal bandwidth per exchange, optimized network traffic, keep data privacy?
  - clients (IoT, edge) far more constrained than data center servers: processing power, memory, storage
  - Q2: efficient FL as devices spread, optimize per-client resources, diverse devices, complex DNNs?
- REFT: variable pruning (by client capacity) + knowledge distillation (communication efficiency, privacy)
  - inspired by FedKD (public dataset for privacy); asynchronous updates + public data
  - experiments: fewer parameters, FLOPs, bandwidth; accuracy comparable to existing FL
- Contributions
  - variable pruning: per-client level, one-shot structured pruning of initial weights at server
  - one-way, one-shot client-to-server distillation on unlabeled, non-sensitive public data; heterogeneous pruned architectures participate
- Overall: efficient, effective FL for constrained devices, better client resource use, diverse architectures

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has made a lot of progress recently in many domains, including image classification and natural language processing, among others. But training complex Deep Neural Network (DNN) models needs massive amounts of data. Training with large data volumes works well in centralized scenarios, where the model can access all of the data. However in most cases, especially in distributed systems with Internet-of-Things (IoT) and edge devices, the data resources are decentralized by nature. This decentralized distribution of data makes collaborative training difficult, mainly because of technical intricacies, privacy concerns, and the intricacies of data ownership. Federated Learning (FL) has come up as a promising solution to these problems, because it allows distributed model training on decentralized data while keeping the data private.

FL techniques allow collaborative training by sharing model parameters, or gradients, again and again during training. The communication is between client devices connected to the Internet, which include IoT and edge devices, and a central server that is remote in the cloud, and together these form an FL-based system. Usually this exchange is done over common protocols like TCP or UDP, or other application layer protocols. After every round of training on its local data, a client sends its model parameters to the central server, and the server aggregates the parameters from all the clients using traditional data aggregation methods. But this iterative process needs a lot of back-and-forth communication between client and server, so bandwidth consumption goes up and communication efficiency goes down. This is a big hurdle for building efficient FL-based systems, especially in resource-constrained environments like smart home setups with IoT and edge devices that have limited hardware resources and simplified web infrastructure. It is challenging to use FL effectively in these applications while also treating data privacy as equally important. To reduce communication bottlenecks in these FL scenarios, some research has worked on reducing communication time and packet loss by optimizing application layer protocols. They look at Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), and ZeroMQ Message Transport Protocol (ZMTP) to make data exchange more efficient.

Even with these advancements there are still challenges in FL-based systems, such as the large number of bidirectional communication rounds, the size of each model update, and concerns about data privacy. This brings us to the following question: How can we do FL with the fewest communication rounds, using as little bandwidth as possible in each exchange and optimizing the overall network traffic, and still keep FL's fundamental principle of data privacy? Also, client devices in FL, like IoT and edge devices, often have far more constrained resources than data center servers, with limits in processing power, memory, and storage. So the next question is: How can we do FL efficiently as IoT and edge devices become more and more common, while optimizing resource usage on each client and supporting a wide range of diverse client devices, especially when we work with complex DNN models?

To address these challenges we propose "Resource-Efficient Federated Training (REFT)", which is a framework that combines variable pruning and knowledge distillation. Variable pruning reduces the model parameters based on the computational capacity of the client, and knowledge distillation improves communication efficiency and data privacy. Our method is inspired by FedKD, which uses a public dataset to reduce privacy concerns. Unlike existing methods, we do asynchronous updates and use public data, which reduces communication and privacy risks. Our experiments show big reductions in parameters, FLOPs, and bandwidth consumption, while accuracy stays comparable to existing FL techniques. Our key contributions are:

- We introduce variable pruning, a framework for applying model pruning techniques where the pruning level is adjusted for each client based on its available computational resources. We do one-shot structured pruning on the initial model weights at the server, and this customizes the pruning level for each client. This uses client resources efficiently and reduces both computational and communication overhead (or keeps them at an acceptable level), so the model is more suitable for training on resource-constrained devices.

- We use a one-way, one-shot client-to-server knowledge distillation approach with unlabeled, non-sensitive public data. This further improves communication efficiency in federated learning by optimizing how knowledge is transferred from the clients to the server. We also support clients with heterogeneous model architectures, which come from the structured pruning, so they can actively participate in training.

Overall, our approach combines variable model pruning and one-shot knowledge distillation to make federated learning more efficient and effective, so it is more feasible for resource-constrained devices, it uses resources on the client side better, and it supports diverse client architectures.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent advancements in deep learning have yielded significant progress across diverse domains, including, but not limited to, image classification and natural language processing. However, training complex Deep Neural Network (DNN) models requires massive amounts of data. Training models with substantial data volumes works well in centralized scenarios where the model has access to all of the data. However, in most cases, particularly in distributed systems involving Internet-of-Things (IoT) and edge devices, data resources are inherently decentralized. This decentralized data distribution presents challenges for collaborative training, stemming mainly from technical intricacies, privacy concerns, and the intricacies of data ownership. In response, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution, enabling distributed model training on decentralized data while maintaining data privacy.

FL techniques facilitate collaborative training by iteratively sharing model parameters, or gradients, during the training process. This communication takes place between client devices connected to the Internet, including IoT and edge devices, and a central server located remotely in the cloud, forming an FL-based system. Typically, this exchange is carried out via widely adopted protocols such as TCP or UDP [1], or alternative application layer protocols [2]. After each round of training on local data, a client transmits its model parameters to the central server, which aggregates these parameters from all clients using traditional data aggregation methods. However, this iterative process requires a significant number of back-and-forth client-server communications, increasing bandwidth consumption and reducing communication efficiency. This poses significant hurdles for establishing efficient FL-based systems, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as smart home setups involving IoT and edge devices with limited hardware resources and simplified web infrastructure. Effectively harnessing FL in such applications while giving equal importance to data privacy is challenging. To alleviate communication bottlenecks in such FL scenarios, some research initiatives [2,1] have focused on reducing communication time and minimizing packet loss by optimizing application layer protocols. Specifically, they explore Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), and ZeroMQ Message Transport Protocol (ZMTP) to improve the efficiency of data exchange.

Despite these advancements, challenges persist in FL-based systems, including the substantial number of bidirectional communication rounds, the size of each model update, and data privacy concerns. This leads us to the following question: How can we execute FL with the fewest communication rounds, minimizing bandwidth consumption in each exchange and optimizing overall network traffic, while preserving FL's fundamental principle of data privacy? Furthermore, client devices in FL, such as IoT and edge devices, often have significantly more constrained resources than data center servers, with limitations in processing power, memory, and storage. This prompts a further question: How can we efficiently execute FL as IoT and edge devices become increasingly prevalent, while optimizing resource usage on each client and accommodating a wide array of diverse client devices, particularly when working with complex DNN models?

To address these challenges, we propose "Resource-Efficient Federated Training (REFT)", a framework that combines variable pruning and knowledge distillation techniques. Variable pruning reduces model parameters based on the client's computational capacity, while knowledge distillation improves communication efficiency and data privacy. Our method is inspired by FedKD [3], which uses a public dataset to mitigate privacy concerns. Unlike existing methods, we perform asynchronous updates and leverage public data, reducing communication and privacy risks. Our experiments demonstrate significant reductions in parameters, FLOPs, and bandwidth consumption while maintaining accuracy comparable to existing FL techniques. We summarize our key contributions as follows:

- • We introduce variable pruning, a framework for applying model pruning techniques that adjusts the pruning level for each client based on its available computational resources. By performing one-shot structured pruning on the initial model weights at the server, we customize the pruning level for each client. This approach uses client resources efficiently and reduces both computational and communication overhead (or keeps them at an acceptable level), making the model more suitable for training on resource-constrained devices.

- • We employ a one-way, one-shot client-to-server knowledge distillation approach using unlabeled, non-sensitive public data. This further enhances communication efficiency in federated learning by optimizing the transfer of knowledge from clients to the server. We also accommodate clients with heterogeneous model architectures, obtained after structured pruning, enabling their active participation in training.

Overall, our approach combines variable model pruning and one-shot knowledge distillation to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of federated learning, making it more feasible for resource-constrained devices, improving resource utilization on the client side, and accommodating diverse client architectures.

References:

[2] Cleland et al . (2022) Gary Cleland, Di Wu, Rehmat Ullah, and Blesson Varghese. 2022. FedComm: Understanding Communication Protocols for Edge-based Federated Learning. arXiv:2208.08764 [cs.DC]
[3] Gong et al . (2022a) Xuan Gong, Abhishek Sharma, Srikrishna Karanam, Ziyan Wu, Terrence Chen, David S. Doermann, and Arun Innanje. 2022a.
